entry.title: Identity Propagation from Joule to SAP SuccessFactors
entry.content:
During workforce management reviews, HR managers and administrators frequently need to audit employee contract extension data. Searching through nested SAP SuccessFactors menus or manually parsing custom Metadata Framework (MDF) objects introduces friction into routine operations.

By integrating Joule with custom extension agents on SAP BTP, users can query sensitive custom MDF objects—such as Contract Renewal entities—using natural language while dynamically enforcing SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP) for every tool call.

Scenario Overview

  • Intent Initiation via Digital Assistant: An HR administrator or standard employee queries Joule using natural language to retrieve or verify contract renewal cases for an employee.
  • Identity Propagation & Session Context: Joule interprets the prompt and executes user identity propagation (principal propagation) down to SAP SuccessFactors, ensuring that the authenticated user's session context is preserved end-to-end.
  • Context-Aware RBP Enforcement: The custom agent fetches data directly from SuccessFactors OData APIs. Access to sensitive fields (such as salary adjustments or contract terms) is governed entirely by the user's assigned SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions.

This article walks through the end-to-end configuration: setting up trust between Joule and SuccessFactors, enabling principal propagation, and enforcing role-based access to the custom Contract Renewal MDF object.

Prerequisites

To successfully implement this architecture, ensure that the following system dependencies and administrative privileges are in place:

  • SAP BTP Subaccount with Joule Enabled: An active subaccount on SAP BTP with the Joule digital assistant entitlement subscribed and provisioned.
  • SAP Identity Authentication Service (IAS): An IAS tenant configured as the Identity Provider for both your SAP BTP subaccount and your SAP SuccessFactors instance to enable OpenID Connect (OIDC) and SAML token exchanges.
  • Custom MDF Object in SuccessFactors: A custom Metadata Framework (MDF) object—such as Contract Renewal—created via Configure Object Definitions in SuccessFactors.
  • Role-Based Permissions (RBP) Configured: Specific permissions assigned in SuccessFactors RBP for the custom MDF object (e.g., read/write access granted to HR Manager, and restricted for Standard User).
  • Administrative Access: Administrator privileges across the SAP BTP Cockpit, the SAP IAS Administration Console, and the SuccessFactors Admin Center.
  • Protocol Familiarity: Basic understanding of OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect (OIDC), JSON Web Tokens (JWT), and SAML 2.0 bearer assertions.

Architecture Overview

The following diagram illustrates the end-to-end trust chain and identity flow between Joule, SAP BTP, SAP Cloud Identity Services, and SAP SuccessFactors:
 
The identity flow begins when a user authenticates in Joule via SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS). Joule’s A2A client routes the prompt through a BTP Destination to the pro-code custom agent on SAP Cloud Foundry. The agent validates and forwards the user token, using a second BTP Destination to execute a SAML Bearer Assertion against SAP SuccessFactors. This ensures the request hits the OData API Center with the user's active session context, dynamically enforcing Role-Based Permissions (RBP) at the backend metadata layer.
 

Generate the SAML Signing Certificate

The BTP Destination Service will sign SAML assertions using a certificate. SuccessFactors needs that certificate registered to trust those assertions. Two commands are needed here because the outputs serve two different purposes and go to two different systems.

The first command generates the raw key material in PEM format — certificate.pem  is the public certificate you upload to SuccessFactors, and privateKey.pem is the private key that stays on your machine.

openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 3650 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout certs/privateKey.pem \
  -out certs/certificate.pem \
  -subj "/CN=sfsf-assistant-saml"

The second command takes those two PEM files and bundles them together into a PKCS#12 keystore (.p12). This is the format BTP Destination Service expects when it needs to sign SAML assertions on behalf of your application — a plain PEM file is not sufficient for this purpose.

openssl pkcs12 -export \
  -in certs/certificate.pem \
  -inkey certs/privateKey.pem \
  -out certs/sfsf-saml-client.p12 \
  -name "sfsf-saml-client" \
  -password pass:yourpassword

certificate.pem goes to SuccessFactors when registering the OAuth2 client. sfsf-saml-client.p12 goes to the BTP Destination Service certificate store. Remember, the password for your .p12 certificate will be required when you use it in the destination configuration. 

Register an OAuth2 Client in SuccessFactors

SuccessFactors needs to know your app's signing certificate before it will accept SAML assertions from it.

1. Log in to SuccessFactors Admin Center. Navigate to Admin Center → Manage OAuth2 Client Applications or Under the tools Search field type Manage OAuth2 Client Applications and click the link in the search results.

2. Click Register Client Application

3. When you click Register Client Application under Manage OAuth2 Client Applications in SAP SuccessFactors, you will need to fill out the following form fields:

  • Company: Pre-filled automatically based on your current SuccessFactors instance or tenant ID.
  • Application Name: A unique, descriptive name for your client application or integration.
  • Description (Optional): A short note explaining the purpose of the application or integration.
  • Application URL: A valid URL pointing to the client application or vendor's website domain.
  • X.509 Certificate: Paste your pre-generated public certificate text which we generated in the previous section.

and click Register

4. After clicking Register, the system generates a public API Key required for authenticating your API requests. To retrieve this key, locate your new client entry in the list, navigate to the Actions column, and click View.

5.Locate the generated API Key. Copy it and store it safely, as your external application will require it to complete the connection.

Maintain the Generated Certificate in BTP Destination Service

Before configuring the destination itself, the .p12 keystore must be uploaded to the BTP Destination Service certificate store. The destination references it by name — it is never embedded inline.

1. Login into the SAP BTP Cockpit and navigate to your Subaccount. Go to Connectivity and navigate directly to Destination Certificates and click on Import Button.

2. Click the Upload button to select your certificate file from your local file system

3. Select sfsf-saml-client.p12  from your local machine and click on Open button.

4. Click on Create button

Once uploaded, the certificate appears in the list with the name sfsf-saml-client.p12. This is the exact value you will enter as Key Store Location when configuring the sfsf-conn destination.

The certificate store is scoped to your BTP subaccount. Multiple destinations in the same subaccount can reference the same uploaded keystore.

Import the Destinations

With the certificate uploaded, you can now create the destination that performs the actual principal propagation. This destination is what your application calls to exchange the user's IAS token for a SuccessFactors OAuth token.
Rather than filling in every property manually, download the pre-built destination file below and import it directly into BTP. You only need to update the four placeholder values specific to your SuccessFactors tenant before importing.

Download: (destinations/sfsf-conn.properties)

Open the file and replace the following placeholders with your own values:

Authentication=OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
KeyStoreLocation=sfsf-saml-client.p12
KeyStorePassword=<keystore-password>
Name=sfsf-conn
ProxyType=Internet
SAMLAssertionProvider=DestinationServiceGenerated
Type=HTTP
URL=<successfactors-api-url>
apiKey=<generated-api-key-in-successfactor>
audience=www.successfactors.com
authnContextClassRef=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PreviousSession
clientKey=<generated-api-key-in-successfactor>
companyId=<company-id-in-successfactor>
includeSigningCertificateInSAMLAssertion=true
nameIdFormat=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:unspecified
skipUserAttributesPrefixInSAMLAttributes=true
skipUserUuidInSAMLAttributes=true
tokenServiceURL=<successfactors-api-url>/oauth/token
tokenServiceURLType=Dedicated
  • <successfactors-api-url>:  SAP  API domain (e.g., api12sales.successfactors.eu) — appears in both URL and tokenServiceURL
  • <generated-api-key-in-successfactor>: The API Key (Client ID) generated during OAuth2 registration in SF — appears in both clientKey and apiKey.
  • <company-id-in-successfactor>:  Your SAP SF company/tenant ID.
  • <keystore-password>:  The password set for the uploaded .p12 X.509 certificate used for SAML signing.

All other properties — authentication type, SAML settings, certificate flags — are already correctly configured in the file. Once you have updated the placeholders, import the file into BTP:

1. Go to BTP Cockpit → Connectivity → Destinations then click Create.

2. In the Create New Destination dialog box, select From File to import an already configured destination.

3. Select sfsf-conn.properties from your local machine, then click Open.

4. Destination successfully imported, Click OK.

5. On the destination detail page, click Check Connection. A successful Check Connection confirms the destination is correctly configured and reachable.

Principal Propagation from Joule to Agent

With Joule’s Pro-Code Extensibility, customers can seamlessly integrate custom, code-based agents into the Joule ecosystem using third-party frameworks—a paradigm known as "Bring Your Own Agent" (BYOA). Rather than relying solely on declarative Joule frameworks, a BYOA agent operates as a standard, code-based application that communicates directly with Joule via the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol. However, extending Joule’s capabilities with custom logic requires careful consideration of how enterprise data is accessed.

For any production-grade agent interacting with core enterprise platforms like SAP SuccessFactors, implementing Principal Propagation (User Identity Propagation) is non-negotiable. Omitting identity propagation forces the agent to execute requests under a generic technical user identity, which inherently bypasses individual Role-Based Permissions (RBP) and exposes the organization to major architectural, security, and governance risks.

With principal propagation active, data authorization is enforced directly at the backend source system layer in SuccessFactors. This guarantees that unauthorized data payloads are stopped at the source and never exposed to intermediate agent layers or the client application — making identity propagation the core mechanism for maintaining strict enterprise compliance.

Achieving this level of security requires building a continuous chain of trust across the SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP). The previous steps established the connection between SAP SuccessFactors and the BTP environment to enable user-propagated API calls. The next phase establishes trust between Joule and the agent. The resulting end-to-end authentication pipeline flows from the Joule-managed SAP Identity Authentication Service (IAS) tenant, through the agent, and directly into SAP SuccessFactors — yielding a stateless, credential-less agent that holds no long-lived backend credentials, ensuring every backend request is executed strictly within the real-time permissions of the logged-in user.

The setup for establishing trust between Joule and the agent follows the foundation outlined by Felix Bartler in his article, Joule A2A: Propagate the User Identity from Joule into S/4HANA. You may follow the steps directly from Felix's guide or proceed with the tailored implementation steps outlined below.

Registering the IAS Applications for App-to-App Trust

IAS acts as the gatekeeper for every token exchange in this chain. Before Joule can hand its token to your agent, IAS needs to know who each participant is and needs explicit authorization for each step in the exchange. That means registering two OpenID Connect applications — one representing the proxy, one representing your agent — and then drawing the permission path between them.

Both applications must be created in the same IAS tenant where your BTP subaccount established trust during Joule provisioning. You can confirm which tenant that is under Subaccount → Security → Trust Configuration.

Create the IAS Applications

In the IAS admin panel, navigate to Applications & Resources → Applications and create two OpenID Connect applications:

1. A2A_Proxy_App — the intermediary that receives Joule's token and hands it forward. After creating it, expose an API resource on the application (e.g., a2a_proxy_app_api). This API defines the audience (aud) claim that exchanged tokens will carry, which IAS uses to validate that the exchange is directed at the right target.

2. A2A_Custom_Agent_Apps — the application representing your actual agent, the one that will call SuccessFactors. Expose an API resource here as well (e.g., a2a_custom_agent_app_api), for the same reason.

Configure the Trust Chain

Dependencies in IAS define which token exchanges are permitted. In this setup, you need to configure two specific application dependencies: the inbound Joule proxy dependency and the downstream target application dependency.

1. Joule → Proxy: Locate the pre-existing Joule IAS application in your tenant. Add a dependency targeting A2A_Proxy_App  and select its exposed API. Name this dependency exactly joule-to-proxy — this string is hardcoded into Joule's runtime and cannot be changed.

2. Proxy → Agent: Open A2A_Proxy_App and add a dependency targeting  A2A_Custom_Agent_App. Name it proxy-to-target. This name is your choice, but you will need to reference it exactly in the BTP Destination configuration in the next section.

Because the joule-to-proxy dependency is fixed to your proxy app once, adding a future agent requires only a new IAS application and a new proxy-to-<name> dependency on the same proxy — no changes to Joule's configuration.

Finally, generate a client secret on A2A_Proxy_App under Client Authentication → Secrets. The BTP Destination Service will use these credentials to authenticate as the proxy when performing the second token exchange. Save the client ID and secret — you will need them in the next section.

Bring Your Own Agent (BYOA) and Extend Joule Capabilities

To simplify building pro-code custom agents for Joule, we leverage the SAP A2A Agent Toolkit — a skill for Claude Code that scaffolds a complete pro-code agent alongside a Joule capability and Cloud Foundry deployment config in a single command. Supporting both Python and TypeScript, it seamlessly integrates with LangGraph and SAP AI Core / GenAI Hub, handling everything from agent creation to A2A protocol wiring and Joule registration. You can explore the skill page and find the source code in the GitHub repository.

For this SAP SuccessFactors scenario, you can build the agent and Joule capability from scratch using the toolkit—or take the faster path by cloning this ready-to-use reference template from GitHub, which comes with principal propagation pre-configured. With just a few environment updates, your agent and Joule capability will be ready for deployment.

git clone https://github.com/alphageek7443/sfsf-assistant.git
cd sfsf-assistant

The project structure includes exactly what the toolkit generates:

  • app/ — Core agent implementation and business logic.
  • joule-capability/ — Joule capability definitions and A2A wiring.
  • manifest.yml —Cloud Foundry deployment specification.

Before deploying, let's update the environment placeholders and configuration properties to match your target BTP and SuccessFactors landscapes.

Updating the Cloud Foundry Manifest

The repository comes pre-configured with a manifest.yml structure matching the output of the SAP A2A Agent Toolkit. Open manifest.yml and adjust the environment variables and service bindings to align with your landscape:

applications:
  - name: sfsf-assistant
    memory: 512M
    disk_quota: 1G
    instances: 1
    buildpacks:
      - python_buildpack
    command: python -m app
    env:
      MODEL_NAME: gpt-4.1
      AICORE_RESOURCE_GROUP: default
      IAS_ISSUER: https://your-ias-tenant.accounts.ondemand.com
      IAS_AUDIENCE: your-ias-audience-uuid
    services:
      - your-destination-service
    routes:
      - route: your-app.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

Key Configuration Placeholders to Update:

  • MODEL_NAME & AICORE_RESOURCE_GROUP: Set these to match your active model deployment name and resource group in SAP AI Core / GenAI Hub (e.g., gpt-4o, gpt-4.1, etc.). Ensure your AI Core service binding or secret is configured in BTP to grant access to this model.
  • IAS_ISSUER: Your IAS tenant URL (e.g., https://.accounts.ondemand.com). This must match the exact IAS tenant where you registered the trust and applications earlier.
  • IAS_AUDIENCE: The Client ID of the A2A_Custom_Agent_App (not the proxy app). This is a critical link back to your IAS setup: the agent middleware uses this value to cryptographically verify that inbound user tokens exchanged by Joule are intended for this specific agent.
  • services: Replace your-destination-service with the actual name of your SAP BTP Destination Service instance bound to your subaccount.
  • routes: Update your-app.cfapps..hana.ondemand.com to match your BTP Cloud Foundry region and confirm the route host is unique within your organization.

Deploying the Custom Agent

Provision the Destination Service instance (if not already created) and push the application to Cloud Foundry:

# Create the destination service instance
cf create-service destination lite sfsf-assistant-dest

# Deploy the custom agent
cf push

Once deployed, take note of your application’s live route URL—we will use it later when configuring the BTP HTTP destination to the custom agent.

Key Implementation Patterns

Three core components in the agent application work together to pass the user's identity from the inbound A2A request all the way into SAP SuccessFactors. The agent logic itself (agent.py) remains completely decoupled from security tokens, while two supporting layers handle identity capture and downstream token exchange.

1. Inbound Identity Capture (main.py)

A Starlette middleware intercepts inbound A2A requests, extracts the bearer token, and validates it against your IAS tenant before storing it in the request context:

class IASAuthMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next):
        auth = request.headers.get("authorization", "")
        token = auth.removeprefix("Bearer ").strip() if auth.startswith("Bearer ") else None

        if token and (claims := _verify_ias_token(token)):
            set_user_token(token)  # Store token in context for active request thread

        return await call_next(request)

During local development, setting IAS_ISSUER and IAS_AUDIENCE to local placeholders bypasses token signature checks so you can test using mock tokens without modifying code.

2. Downstream Token Exchange (sfsf_client.py)

When tools fetch data from SuccessFactors, sfsf_client.py retrieves the context token and passes it to the SAP BTP Destination Service via the X-user-token header:

def get_sfsf_token_and_url() -> tuple[str, str]:
    creds = _get_dest_service_creds()
    user_token = get_user_token()

    # Get Destination Service access token
    ds_token = httpx.post(
        f"{creds['url']}/oauth/token",
        data={"grant_type": "client_credentials"},
        auth=(creds["clientid"], creds["clientsecret"]),
    ).json()["access_token"]

    # Request SuccessFactors token with user identity attached
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {ds_token}"}
    if user_token:
        headers["X-user-token"] = user_token  # Triggers SAML assertion for end-user

    dest = httpx.get(
        f"{creds['uri']}/destination-configuration/v1/destinations/sfsf-conn",
        headers=headers,
    ).json()

    return dest["authTokens"][0]["value"], dest["destinationConfiguration"]["URL"].rstrip("/")

Why X-user-token matters: Supplying the X-user-token header instructs the Destination Service to generate a user-bound SAML assertion. If omitted, the service falls back to the technical user configured on the destination, bypassing SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP).

Agent Tool Decoupling (agent.py)

Because the middleware and HTTP client manage identity propagation transparently, tools invoke standard OData calls directly:

@tool
def get_contract_renewal_cases(
    employee_id: str | None = None,
    status: str | None = None,
    department: str | None = None,
    faculty: str | None = None,
    top: int = 5,
) -> dict:
    """Fetch contract renewal cases from SuccessFactors.

    Use this tool to look up employment contract renewals, renewal dates, salary
    adjustments, performance grades, approval/review workflow status, and case notes
    for employees. Also covers vendor agreements and internal service transfers.

    Args:
        employee_id: Filter by employee userId (e.g. '103266'). Use userId, not username — resolve via search_employees first if needed.
        status:      Filter by case status (e.g. 'READY_FOR_SS_REVIEW', 'SS_REVIEWED_APPROVED', 'HRP_VALIDATED')
        department:  Filter by department code (e.g. 'ME')
        faculty:     Filter by faculty code (e.g. 'FoE')
        top:         Maximum number of results to return (default 5)
    """
    filters = []
    if employee_id:
        filters.append(f"cust_Employee eq '{employee_id}'")
    if status:
        filters.append(f"cust_status eq '{status}'")
    if department:
        filters.append(f"cust_department eq '{department}'")
    if faculty:
        filters.append(f"cust_faculty eq '{faculty}'")

    params = {
        "$select": (
            "externalCode,externalName,cust_Employee,cust_department,cust_faculty,"
            "cust_designation,cust_currentSalary,cust_newSalary,cust_salaryAdjustment,"
            "cust_performanceGrade,cust_currentEndDate,cust_proposedEndDate,"
            "cust_durationMonths,cust_discussionDate,cust_status,cust_notes,"
            "lastModifiedDateTime,lastModifiedBy,createdDateTime,createdBy"
        ),
        "$orderby": "lastModifiedDateTime desc",
        "$top": str(top),
    }
    if filters:
        params["$filter"] = " and ".join(filters)

    result = sfsf_get("/odata/v2/cust_ContractRenewalCaseV2", params)

    if isinstance(result, dict) and not result.get("error"):
        records = result.get("d", {}).get("results", [])
        if not records:
            return {
                "message": "No contract renewal cases found",
                "filters_applied": {
                    "employee_id": employee_id,
                    "status": status,
                    "department": department,
                    "faculty": faculty,
                },
            }

    return result

Configure and Deploy the Joule Capability

Open joule-capability/capability.sapdas.yaml. The system_aliases block maps a logical name to a BTP destination. The destination name here must exactly match the name of the BTP destination you will create in the next section to point Joule at your agent:

system_aliases:
  SfsfAssistant:
    destination: sfsf-assistant-auth

Leave it as sfsf-assistant-auth unless you plan to use a different destination name—just make sure they match. Next, navigate to the capability directory, authenticate, and deploy the capability to Joule:

Register the Joule Capability

With the agent running, register the capability with Joule:

cd joule-capability
joule deploy -c ./da.sapdas.yaml -n sfsf_assistant_a2a

This compiles and publishes the capability to your Joule tenant. Once the BTP destination is in place, Joule will be able to route user prompts directly to your custom agent.

Configuring the BTP HTTP Destination (Joule -> Custom Agent)

To execute the downstream authentication flow, construct an HTTP destination in your SAP BTP subaccount using the OAuth2JWTBearer authentication type. This destination incorporates specific properties that instruct the SAP BTP Destination Service to execute the token exchange.

Rather than filling in every property manually, download the pre-built destination file below and import it directly into BTP. You only need to update the placeholder values.

Download: (destinations/sfsf-assistant-auth.properties)

Open the file and replace the following placeholders with your own values:

Destination Configuration Parameters

Configure the destination with the following properties:

Name=sfsf-assistant-auth
Type=HTTP
ProxyType=Internet
Authentication=OAuth2JWTBearer
URL=<your-agent-route>
clientId=<A2A_Proxy_App-client-id>
clientSecret=<A2A_Proxy_App-client-secret>
tokenServiceURL=https://<your-ias-tenant>/oauth2/token
tokenServiceURLType=Dedicated
apptoapp=true
tokenService.body.token_format=jwt
tokenService.body.client_id=<A2A_Proxy_App-client-id>
tokenService.body.resource=urn:sap:identity:application:provider:name:proxy-to-target
tokenService.addClientCredentialsInBody=false
x_user_token.jwks_uri=https://<your-ias-tenant>/oauth2/certs

Four placeholders to fill in:

  • <your-agent-route>:  The Cloud Foundry route URL of your deployed custom agent.
  • <A2A_Proxy_App-client-id>: The Client ID generated for A2A_Proxy_App in IAS -- appears in clientId and tokenService.body.client_id
  • <A2A_Proxy_App-client-secret>:  The Client secret generated for A2A_Proxy_App in IAS
  • <your-ias-tenant>:  Your IAS tenant domain -- appears in tokenServiceURL and x_user_token.jwks_uri

Note: The Name property must exactly match the destination referenced in capability.sapdas.yaml (sfsf-assistant-auth). If you customized the destination alias in your capability file, ensure it matches here character-for-character.

Key Architectural Highlights & Considerations

Proxy Client Credentials: The clientId and clientSecret parameters correspond to the IAS proxy application (A2A_Proxy_App), not the custom agent itself. This destination handles the token assertion request sent to the custom agent. Joule automatically manages the initial authentication flow before resolving this destination.

Dependency Mapping (tokenService.body.resource): This property targets the IAS dependency name. The prefix urn:sap:identity:application:provider:name: must be prepended to the exact target application dependency configured in IAS (e.g., proxy-to-target).

User Token Validation (x_user_token.jwks_uri): This parameter points to the JWKS endpoint of your IAS tenant, enabling the SAP BTP Destination Service to cryptographically validate the inbound end-user token before issuing the downstream assertion. Warning: Omitting x_user_token.jwks_uri causes the Destination Service to fail user token validation and silently fall back to a technical service user, breaking end-to-end principal propagation.

App-to-App Mode (apptoapp=true): Explicitly enables App2App authentication mode within the SAP BTP Destination Service.

End-to-End Execution Flow & Testing

To verify that principal propagation and capability routing function correctly across the entire integration, we test the end-to-end flow in Joule using two distinct user personas with contrasting SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP).

For a visual step-by-step walkthrough, you can watch the video demonstration below or review the conversation screenshots in the following subsections.

Multi-Persona Verification Highlights

HR Manager Persona (Tessa Walker): When logged in as HR Manager Tessa Walker, the custom agent leverages full authorized access to sensitive employee compensation and contract data:

Broad Query & Disambiguation: Tessa prompts Joule to show contract renewal cases and requests details for a specific employee. The agent detects multiple active employee records associated with the target employee, prompts for clarification, and asks the user to select the target record.

Detailed Record Retrieval: Upon selecting the specific user record, the propagated user identity passes through the BTP Destination service and returns comprehensive contract renewal details, including Case ID, Department, Designation, Faculty, Current Salary, New Salary, Duration, HRP Validation Status, and Performance Grade.

 

Standard User Persona (Benney Cobb): When executing the exact same conversation flow as a standard employee, principal propagation ensures that security boundaries are strictly maintained:

Directory Resolution vs. Restricted Contracts: Benney initiates the same query for the employee. While Benney's RBP correctly permits basic user directory lookups (successfully resolving the employee's name to the matching user IDs), subsequent calls to the sensitive contract entities fail to return records due to a lack of HR management privileges.

Controlled Output: After specifying the target record, Joule responds cleanly stating that no contract renewal cases were found for the selected user ID. This verifies that security and RBP are enforced at the backend OData layer without requiring custom authorization logic.
 

Conclusion

Extending Joule with pro-code custom agents via the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol unlocks powerful, enterprise-grade extensibility patterns on SAP BTP. By leveraging Bring Your Own Agent (BYOA) architectures, development teams can build tailored AI agents using tools like LangGraph while maintaining strict security boundaries.

Integrating the SAP BTP Destination Service with App-to-App (App2App) token exchange and X-user-token propagation guarantees that every AI-driven tool call respects SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP). This ensures end-to-end data security, user context preservation, and full auditability without compromising the developer experience.

References

  • SAP A2A Agent Toolkit
  • SAP A2A Agent Toolkit GitHub Repository
  • Joule A2A: Propagate the User Identity from Joule into S/4HANA

entry.title: How Komatsu Accelerated S/4HANA 2023 with Clean Core and SAP Joule for Developers
entry.content:
Implementing Clean Core Governance on S/4HANA 2023: Lessons from the Field

We work on the SAP team at Komatsu, one of the world's largest manufacturers of construction and mining equipment. Over the past year, we have been running an S/4HANA 2023 transformation program and set up a Clean Core governance model from scratch. This post shares the technical decisions, configuration steps, and practical lessons from that work, specifically the A-D object classification, ATC setup on S/4HANA 2023, Cloudification Repository usage, and how we remediated Level C and D findings.

Why Clean Core Matters for Upgrade Safety

Before our transformation, Komatsu's ECC landscape had accumulated hundreds of custom objects User Exits, BAdIs, Business Transaction Events (BTEs), VOFM Routines, and Web Dynpro screens. Each one is a potential blocker during an S/4HANA upgrade. SAP Clean Core is not a product; it is a strategy: keep the S/4HANA digital core as close to standard as possible and route business-specific extensions outside the core using loosely coupled patterns on SAP BTP.

The fundamental architectural shift this requires is moving computation from the ABAP application server down to SAP HANA. Classic SELECT * with joins and internal table processing needs to be replaced by CDS View entities, ABAP RAP business objects, and AMDP-based pushdown logic. This is not just a syntax change it requires developers to think differently about where logic runs.

The SAP Innovation Cycle: Six-Step Transformation Framework

A six-phase, AI-augmented approach that moves from initial exploration through to a fully upgrade-ready, AI-integrated digital core. The following phases reflect how we structured our own program this is not an official SAP methodology.

 

 

Here, the goal is not just to prepare the system for future innovations, but to make it truly AI-ready empowering us to harness the value of AI today while building a foundation for the breakthroughs of tomorrow.

The Four-Level Classification Framework (A-D)

The core of our governance model is a four-level extensibility classification aligned with SAP Note #3578329 and the Cloudification Repository Viewer. Every custom object is classified based on upgrade risk before any development begins.

  • SAP Clean Core Governance Framework

Table 1: Clean Core extensibility levels per SAP Note #3578329

Level

Name

Upgrade Risk

Examples

A

Gold Standard

Zero

Cloud-released APIs, Key User Extensibility, Developer Extensibility (ABAP Cloud), BTP Side-By-Side

B

Classic

Low

RAP BOs, CDS Views, CDS Table Functions, AMDP Methods, Cloud-Released BAdIs, Classes/Interfaces

C

Internal Objects

Medium

SAP Internal Objects, BDC, SAP Queries (SQ00/SQ01)

D

Not Recommended

High

Implicit/Explicit Enhancements, VOFM Pricing Routines, Web Dynpro ABAP

Every new requirement first goes through a Fit-to-Standard check. If standard SAP covers the requirement, no custom development is initiated. If a genuine gap exists, the requirement is routed through our governance decision tree. Level A on-stack options (Key User Extensibility, Developer Extensibility) are evaluated first; if not possible, Level B patterns (RAP, CDS, AMDP) are used. Level C and D objects require explicit approval and are added to an upgrade watch list for remediation in the next release cycle.

ATC Configuration for S/4HANA 2023 FPS03

One of the first practical challenges we encountered: the clean core ATC checks are not natively available in S/4HANA 2023. They are delivered out of the box only from S/4HANA 2025. For 2023 systems, you need to implement the following SAP Notes in order.

  • SAP Note 3565942:  Delivers the 'Usage of APIs' and 'Allowed Enhancement Technologies' ATC checks to S/4HANA 2023 systems
  • SAP Note 3627152: Note Analyzer files and bug fixes for the clean core checks; run the Note Analyzer after implementation to verify all recommended notes are current
  • SAP Note 3593439: Excludes key-user-generated objects from clean core ATC findings so they are not wrongly flagged as Level C

After implementing Note 3565942, open the check object SYCM_USAGE_OF_APIS in ADT for Eclipse and choose 'Import Parameters.' This step is easy to miss without it, the check does not have the API classification data it needs to run.

The prebuilt ABAP_CLEAN_CORE_DEVELOPMENT check variant is only available for ATC on SAP BTP or for S/4HANA 2025 FPS01 and above. On 2023, you build the variant manually: go to transaction ATC > Manage Check Variants > Global, copy ABAP_CLOUD_DEVELOPMENT_DEFAULT, and name it (we used ATC_CHECK_RWSMD). Then manually add the 'Usage of APIs' and 'Allowed Enhancement Technologies' checks under the Clean Core category, along with SYCM_ALLOWED_ENH_TECHNOLOGY. Keep the variant focused bundling in unrelated ATC checks causes problems because the RISE Methodology dashboard ignores them and the export can exceed the 100 MB import limit.

Since S/4HANA 2023 qualifies as '2023 and above,' you can run ATC locally via transaction ATC and export the results as a ZIP file (Scenario 1 — Local ATC Check). Import the file into Cloud ALM via: CALM Home > Services > SAP Readiness Check > Create New Analysis. Pre-requisite: the ALM_DEVELOPER role must be assigned to the user in Cloud ALM.

Using the Cloudification Repository to Resolve Level C and D Findings

The SAP Cloudification Repository Viewer is the practical tool for finding successors to deprecated or restricted APIs. When ATC flags an object, we use the repository to check whether a clean alternative exists before deciding how to handle it. The viewer is available at GitHub: sap.github.io/abap-atc-cr-cv-s4hc

Level D example BAPI replacement: We had a use of BAPI_CUSTOMER_GETDETAIL2 flagged as Level D. Checking the Cloudification Repository, the successor is the classic API CL_MDBPCVI_READER. We replaced the BAPI call with this class.

Not every Level D finding has a clean successor. We encountered a direct table update that was flagged Level D, but the code was deployed as part of SAP Note 0001790318. In cases like this, the governance process requires the developer to document that no alternative exists before the object receives an approval exception.

Level C example Table-to-CDS replacement: Several custom objects were flagged because developers used database tables directly instead of released CDS Views. The fix is straightforward once you know the mapping. The following table lists the replacements we applied based on the Cloudification Repository.

Table 2: Direct table references replaced with released CDS Views (source: Cloudification Repository Viewer, S/4HANA 2023 SP2)

Original Table

Released CDS View Replacement

AUFK (Maintenance Orders — AIFH)

I_MaintenanceOrder

MARA (Material)

I_producttp_2

CRMS4_SERV_H (Service Document)

I_SERVICEDOCUMENT

EQUI (Equipment)

I_Equipment

VBAK (Sales Document Header)

I_SalesDocument

VBAP (Sales Document Item)

I_SalesDocumentItem

Any object classified as Level C or D is registered on our upgrade watch list. This ensures technical debt is tracked and remediation is planned before the next S/4HANA version cycle, rather than discovered during the upgrade.

Code Pushdown: The Architectural Shift Developers Need to Internalize

Governance frameworks only work if developers understand the underlying architectural principle. In ECC, computation happened on the ABAP application server SELECT * queries pulled large datasets, and joins, loops, and aggregations ran in ABAP. In S/4HANA, the right model pushes logic down to SAP HANA using CDS Views and RAP. The application server becomes thin; HANA does the heavy lifting in-memory.

Table 3: ECC vs. S/4HANA computation model

Dimension

ECC Approach

S/4HANA Approach

Computation Layer

ABAP Application Server (joins, loops, aggregations)

SAP HANA in-memory DB via CDS Views and RAP

Data Transfer

SELECT * pulls millions of rows to app server

Only small, aggregated result set returned

Resource Consumption

High memory and CPU on application server

Thin logic heavy lifting delegated to database

UI Layer

SAP GUI / classic ABAP reports

SAP Fiori UI (RAP-based applications)

SAP Joule for Developers: Practical Experience

We integrated SAP Joule for Developers (J4D) SAP's AI co-pilot within the development environment to support clean core-compliant development. J4D is useful for several tasks: generating ABAP unit tests, producing RAP business object scaffolding, suggesting CDS-based refactoring for classic SELECT patterns, and explaining complex legacy ABAP code during knowledge transfer sessions.

Based on our internal observations on Level A and B extensibility objects new RAP-based developments where developers followed the clean core patterns we saw noticeably faster throughput compared to manual RICEFW development. We have not formally measured this against a controlled baseline, so we treat the improvement as a qualitative observation rather than a published metric.

J4D operates across two surfaces: SAP Build Code (pro-code, ABAP Cloud environment) for developer extensibility and RAP/wrapper object development, and SAP Build Apps (low-code) for key user extensibility and Fiori application generation.

 

Governance Decision Tree in Practice

Every new requirement goes through this routing logic before a single line of code is written:

1. Introduction

SAP Joule for Consultants is a generative AI copilot built specifically for the SAP consulting community. Grounded in over 9 terabytes of curated SAP knowledge — including 18+ million pages of SAP documentation, 100+ SAP certifications, and implementation guides — it delivers expert-level answers based on trusted SAP content.

But every consulting organization carries its own body of knowledge: internal delivery frameworks, proprietary accelerators, client-specific runbooks, architecture decisions, and hard-won lessons that simply don't exist in SAP's public content. Custom knowledge grounding is what bridges that gap — allowing you to connect Joule to your organization's curated content so it can answer not just as an SAP expert, but as your team's expert.

What Custom Knowledge Grounding Does

Custom Knowledge Grounding extends SAP Joule for Consultants with your organization’s own documents. The documents are uploaded to a data repository, indexed by SAP AI Core Document Grounding, and retrieved at runtime to ground SAP Joule for Consultants’ answers. Users get responses that combine the SAP-curated content SAP Joule for Consultants ships with and their firm’s own methodologies, policies, and delivery standards.

Configuring custom knowledge grounding manually, however, involves its own set of connected steps — setting up the right services, connecting knowledge sources, configuring trust and authorization, and ensuring everything is wired together correctly in the right sequence. Done manually, this takes considerable time and leaves room for misses and misconfiguration.

Cloud Integration Automation Service (CIAS) changes that. entry.title: Anomaly Detection with AI in SAP Cloud ALM for Operations
entry.content:
Introduction

Static thresholds are the weak spot of most monitoring setups. Set them too tight and operations teams drown in alerts. Set them too loose and a real problem slips through until a user calls the service desk. And a value that is perfectly normal on a Monday morning can be a warning sign on a Sunday night.

SAP Cloud ALM for Operations now addresses this with a set of AI capabilities that learn what "normal" looks like for your landscape and flag deviations from it. In this post I give an overview of these capabilities, explain how they fit together from detection to resolution, and share practical tips from customer projects on getting started.

What SAP Cloud ALM offers today

The AI capabilities are not a separate product. They are built into the existing monitoring use cases and fall into three groups: detecting anomalies, recommending thresholds, and helping to resolve alerts.

Use caseCapabilityWhat it does

Health Monitoring

Dynamic Thresholds

Calculates thresholds automatically from historical data and trend analysis, so the system learns the normal behavior of a metric and flags deviations.

Real User Monitoring

Change point detection and seasonal anomaly suppression

Detects significant changes in user-facing performance. Alerts caused by predictable patterns, such as weekly peaks or quarter-end spikes, can be suppressed.

Integration & Exception Monitoring

Anomaly detection on message volume

The event "Anomaly Detected in the Number of Messages Processed" fires when a business service processes more or fewer messages than expected within a time period.

Integration & Exception Monitoring

AI-recommended thresholds

Uses machine learning on historical message counts to suggest threshold values, shown with a trend chart of past volumes.

Business Process Monitoring

AI threshold recommendations

Analyzes the last seven days of document volumes and suggests KPI event thresholds for review.

Alert Management

ALM Alert Resolution Agent

Analyzes alert details, error messages, thresholds and system context, searches documentation, KBAs and SAP Notes, and suggests troubleshooting steps on the Alert Details page.

Dashboards

ALM Dashboard Generation Agent

Creates dashboard cards from system and service data using natural-language prompts.

 

In Health Monitoring, the Quality column shows how far each metric's model has come:

  • Predictive: the model is actively generating thresholds.
  • Learning: more data is being collected.
  • Static: the metric behaves too constantly for a reliable prediction.
  • Insufficient: there is not enough suitable data for predictive modeling.

SAP positions these features as steps toward "Autonomous ALM": from dynamic thresholds and change point detection today toward continuous detection of critical situations, guided resolution with Joule and, eventually, automated remediation.

How it works

 

The monitoring use cases collect the data, the AI layer learns what is normal and flags deviations, and Alert Management routes the result to the right team. The Alert Resolution Agent then supports the first analysis, so the team starts with context instead of a bare alert.

Getting started

The AI capabilities build on a working monitoring setup. If data is already flowing into SAP Cloud ALM, you can start in a few steps:

  1. Connect your systems and services. Anomaly detection needs history, so the earlier data collection starts, the sooner the models have something to learn from.
  2. Activate the monitoring use cases you want to use: Health Monitoring, Real User Monitoring, Integration & Exception Monitoring or Business Process Monitoring.
  3. Switch selected metrics to dynamic thresholds in Health Monitoring, and check the Quality column until they reach "Predictive".
  4. Use "Recommend" for anomaly events in Integration & Exception Monitoring. Review the suggested values against the trend chart, apply them, and regenerate them when the behavior of the monitored service changes.
  5. Accept or adjust the KPI threshold recommendations in Business Process Monitoring.
  6. Route the resulting alerts through Alert Management and Intelligent Event Processing to the right teams via email, Microsoft Teams or your ITSM tool.
  7. Use the ALM Alert Resolution Agent on the Alert Details page to speed up the first analysis.

Lessons from customer projects

  • Start where the noise is. Begin with the metrics and interfaces that generate the most false alerts today. That is where dynamic thresholds pay off fastest and win the trust of the operations team.
  • Give the models time. A metric in "Learning" or "Insufficient" state is not a configuration error. Keep static thresholds in place for critical metrics until the model is predictive.
  • Treat recommendations as a starting point. AI-recommended thresholds are based on past behavior. If the past contains an incident, review the values before you apply them.
  • Decide who gets which alert before go-live. Detection is only half the job. Agree with the Basis, integration and application teams which alerts go to whom and through which channel.
  • Mind the scope for non-SAP systems. Anomaly detection works on the data that reaches SAP Cloud ALM. Third-party systems need to be connected first, for example via OpenTelemetry.

entry.title: Monitoring Dashboards in SAP Cloud ALM for Operations
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP Cloud ALM for Operations collects data from many monitoring use cases, each in its own app. But most people start their day with one question: is everything running, and if not, where do I need to look?

The Monitoring Dashboards app answers that question on a single page. This post shows the predefined dashboards, how to build your own, and how Joule creates dashboard cards from a prompt.

Dashboard options in SAP Cloud ALM

The Monitoring Dashboards app comes with predefined pages and lets you build your own on top of them.

DashboardTypeWhat it shows

Operational Status

Predefined

The status of applications, jobs and integrations in one place

Services Status

Predefined

Service status based on Health Monitoring, Real User Monitoring and Integration & Exception Monitoring

Chart Examples

Predefined

The available chart types, as a reference for your own cards

Personalized dashboard

Custom

Cards from a predefined card library, combining analytics from all Operations apps

Predefined pages cannot be edited directly. To customize one, duplicate it and edit the copy.

Besides the Monitoring Dashboards app, each monitoring use case has its own embedded analytics, without extra configuration. For reporting outside SAP Cloud ALM, the data can be consumed in SAP Analytics Cloud, Grafana or any tool that uses the Analytics API or the OpenTelemetry-based Raw Data Outbound APIs.

How it fits together

The monitoring use cases deliver the data, the Monitoring Dashboards app turns it into pages for each audience, and the same data can also flow to external analytics tools.

Building your first dashboard

  1. Define the audience and the question, for example "Are our order-to-cash integrations healthy right now?"
  2. Duplicate a predefined page such as Operational Status or Services Status and give the copy a clear name.
  3. Add cards from the card library that answer your question, and remove everything else. Use the Chart Examples page to pick the right chart type.
  4. Review it with the users after their first week and adjust it.

AI-generated dashboards with Joule

With the ALM Dashboard Generation Agent, you no longer need to assemble every card by hand. You describe in natural language what you want to see, and Joule creates graphical dashboard cards from your system and service data in SAP Cloud ALM. The agent is generally available, and SAP estimates that it cuts the effort to create and maintain dashboards by 75%.

Prerequisites:

  • The SAP Business AI feature "ALM Dashboard Generation Agent" must be activated.
  • Joule agents are part of SAP Business AI Premium and consume AI Units.

Example prompts you could try:

  • "Show me the number of open alerts per system for the last 7 days."
  • "Create a card with the status of all integrations of business service Order to Cash."
  • "Show the response time trend of our most used Fiori apps."

Conclusion

The Monitoring Dashboards app turns the many monitoring use cases of SAP Cloud ALM into one view per audience, and with Joule a new card is only one sentence away.

Which dashboards do your operations teams use every day? Share your favorite card or prompt in the comments.

FAQ 8 questions

Do I need Joule to use the Second Brain? ▾
Yes — the initialization wizard runs inside SAP Joule Work (or any Claude Code-compatible AI). Once your vault is set up, you also use Joule as the AI that reads and writes to your vault during daily work. The vault itself is just a folder on your local machine.
 
What happens to my data — is it sent to the cloud? ▾
Your vault files live on your local machine. During a Joule session the AI reads the files you open as context, but the files themselves are never uploaded or stored externally. Follow standard SAP data protection guidelines (DPP) for what you share with AI tools — in particular, do not record or share content from meetings with external parties (customers, partners).
 
How long does the initial setup take? ▾
The 9-step wizard takes approximately 10–15 minutes. The AI creates all folders and deploys all skills automatically — you only answer questions and confirm choices. Once done your vault is immediately usable.
 
Can I use the vault for non-HANA topics? ▾
Yes. The vault is role-specific but topic-agnostic. It can hold SAP Notes, BTP documentation, S/4HANA content, meeting notes, emails, and any other artifact you want to distil and retrieve. The HANA-enhanced profiles simply add extra skills for HANA-specific workflows on top of the universal package.
 
How do I update a note when the source document changes? ▾
Drop the updated source into 00_Inbox and run the intake skill. The AI distils the new version and updates the last_reviewed timestamp. For SAP Notes it diffs against the existing note and appends new content only, preserving your existing annotations.
 
Can I share my vault with a colleague? ▾
You can share individual distilled notes (as .md files) and the offline HTML boards. Do not share the full vault folder externally — it may contain customer-confidential content in 05_Cases/. Use the confidentiality-scrub skill before sharing any content outside SAP.
 
What is the "0 fabricated" standard? ▾
Every distilled note from a verified source carries a declaration: "0 fabricated — all content verified against the source document." SAP Note numbers, parameter names, and view names are copied verbatim from the source — the AI never infers or invents them. This is the trust property that makes distilled notes usable in customer communications and escalation discussions.
 
How is this different from SAP's standard Joule features? ▾
Standard Joule answers questions from its training data. Your Second Brain adds your personal knowledge: cases you worked, SAP Notes you read, whiteboards you drew, customer situations you resolved. The AI then answers from your expertise — not generic SAP documentation. The vault is the difference between a fresh Joule session and an expert-calibrated Joule session.

entry.title: Finding Your Joule Work Desktop Admin URL via SAP for Me
entry.content:
Finding Your Joule Work Desktop Admin URL in SAP for Me

When setting up or troubleshooting Joule Work Desktop, you need the Admin URL. Rather than relying on a bookmarked link — which can become outdated as tenants are updated or migrated — the always-current source of truth is SAP for Me. Here's how to find it.

Why Not Just Bookmark the URL?

The Joule Work Desktop Admin URL can change over time — for example after tenant migrations, infrastructure updates, or re-provisioning. A saved link may silently stop working. Going back to SAP for Me ensures you always get the current, valid URL for your landscape.

Step-by-Step: Find the Current URL in SAP for Me

  1. Open SAP for Me and navigate to Portfolio & Products in the left sidebar.
  2. Click the My Product Packages tab. Depending on your screen width, it may be visible directly in the tab bar or accessible via the More dropdown on the right.
  3. In the left panel, click Customer Landscape — this takes you directly to your landscape without having to open an individual Category first.
  4. Find and expand the formation you used for your Core Components activation (Formation Type: Integration with Joule Core). The formation name typically starts with sap-joule-core but may vary depending on how it was set up in your landscape.
  5. In the Systems table, locate the row with System Type Joule Work Desktop.
  6. The URL column contains your current Admin URL — click the external link icon to open it directly.

The Joule Work Desktop URL found under the sap-joule-core formation in Customer Landscape.

 

Tip: Bookmark this SAP for Me page instead of the Admin URL itself — that way you always navigate to the live link rather than a potentially stale one.
